name: rectangular-block
intent: Format every block so that its extent and nesting level are visible at a glance - delimiters aligned as the corners of a rectangle, a compound body on its own indented line - and keep the rectangle narrow by extracting a step or bailing out early instead of nesting further.
problem: Control flow is written as one flat run of statements: compound bodies sit on the header line or wrap arbitrarily, so the shape of the code no longer shows where a block starts and ends, how deep the nesting is, or which statements run unconditionally - the reader has to reconstruct the structure instead of seeing it.
context: Applies wherever code is read more often than it is written: long-lived codebases, review-heavy workflows and teams that want layout decided once rather than per change. It matters most in brace-delimited languages where block shape is a convention rather than syntax and a formatter can enforce the agreed shape; in Go, Rust, Python or Swift the grammar or the first-party toolchain already fixes most of it, so only the depth budget remains.
benefits: Gross structure is readable at a glance: nesting depth shows up as an indentation profile, so a reader sees which statements are conditional before reading a single identifier.

Depth becomes self-limiting: every level consumes visible width, so over-nested code looks wrong and the pressure resolves as extraction (Composed Method) or early exit (Guard Clause) instead of one more level.
Diff hygiene: a deterministic, tool-enforced shape removes whitespace-only review noise so real changes stand out.
Cheaper reviews: the block outline carries the control-flow summary, so a reviewer scans shapes instead of reconstructing branches.

Composes with the sibling formatting patterns (Indented Control Flow, Conditional Expression, Simple Enumeration Parameter, Inline Message) so a method reads top to bottom as a sequence of aligned blocks.
tradeoffs: Vertical space for horizontal clarity: putting every compound body on its own line multiplies rows, which costs screen and diff space - Beck's own forces list records length as a real counter-pressure to readability.
The convention has no runtime effect and, outside Go and Rust, no compiler enforcement: without a formatter wired into CI it decays into churn and reviewer opinion.
Rectangles push code left by design, and the remedy trades nested structure for call structure: extraction produces more small methods, guard clauses produce more exit points, both add indirection.

Wrapped expressions defeat the shape: a long condition or call chain forces continuation lines whose indentation is easily mistaken for a nesting level, so the convention pressures you to introduce named temporaries.
Tool-owned layout couples the codebase to a formatter version and configuration; an upgrade or a conflicting .editorconfig reformats the world and buries the real diff.
In mixed-toolchain repositories (C/C++ subsystems, polyglot monorepos) two teams with different style files cannot share patches without whitespace conflicts.

participants.responsibility: The compound statement - if/else, loop, lambda body, method body - whose extent must be visible as one rectangle, from its opening to its closing delimiter.
The single, uniform displacement applied exactly once per nesting level, which makes depth countable and comparable across the file.
The project's line-length limit; when a rectangle would overrun it, the budget forces extraction or an early exit rather than another nesting level.

The formatter and its committed configuration (gofmt, rustfmt, clang-format, dotnet format, google-java-format, Prettier, ktlint, RuboCop, scalafmt) - and, where none exists, the reviewer reading the diff.

use_cases: Adopting a house style for a codebase that is opening up to outside contributors: pin a formatter configuration (indent step, brace style, line width) and run it in CI, so block shape stops being a review topic.
Reviewing a legacy method with five levels of nesting: read the indentation profile first, then flatten with guard clauses and composed methods until every block fits the width budget.
Code review in a narrow diff view, where the reader sees one column: a rectangular body makes it obvious which statements are inside a branch and which are not.
Teaching or pair-programming: the shape carries the control-flow summary, so discussion starts at the branch that matters instead of at re-indentation.

Configuring a polyglot repository so each language uses its canonical enforcer (gofmt, rustfmt, dotnet format, google-java-format, Prettier, ktlint, RuboCop, scalafmt, clang-format) and the same rule holds across the tree.
A Go repository that runs gofmt in editor hooks or pre-commit: its canonical layout makes block and indentation shapes comparable while keeping diffs focused on real changes.
A Rust repository that pins a rustfmt version and configuration: the official formatter makes block boundaries and line-width decisions repeatable instead of leaving them to reviewer preference.
A JavaScript or TypeScript repository that runs Prettier: its behavior-preserving printer standardizes braces, indentation, and wrapping so a review can focus on control-flow changes.
avoid_when: Generated code, vendored sources or bundled artifacts: nobody reads their shape and reformatting them creates diff noise on every regeneration.
Throwaway scripts and spikes whose only reader is the author for the next hour; the convention buys nothing and the formatting pass costs time.
A repository with an enforced external style (kernel subsystem, vendor SDK, org-wide formatter config): apply the local rule instead, or reformat in a dedicated mechanical commit.
Code where width rather than nesting dominates - wide data tables, long literals, generated DSL blocks - because the rectangle cannot be kept and forcing it hides the data.
anti_patterns: Indentation that imitates structure: continuation lines of a wrapped expression indented like a nested block, so the eye reads a level that does not exist.
Aesthetic churn: reformatting files the change does not otherwise touch, which destroys blame and hides the real diff.
Trusting the rectangle as a substitute for depth control: an aligned six-level block is still unreadable.
Hand-maintained alignment (spaces before = or before trailing comments) that any formatter destroys and that breaks under the next rename.
Extracting one-line helpers only to satisfy the width budget (rectangle theatre), which moves logic out of sight instead of flattening it.
design_principles: Readability over brevity: the pattern optimizes quick and detailed readability and treats line count as the subordinate force.
One level of abstraction per method (Composed Method): a flat body is the visual consequence, and extraction is the remedy when a rectangle grows.
Fail fast at the top (Guard Clause): reject invalid cases before the normal path so the body stays at one indentation level.
Consistency as a design property: one shape for one meaning, applied mechanically by tooling rather than re-decided per change.
best_practices: Let a formatter own the shape: commit the configuration (indent width, brace style, line width) and run the tool in pre-commit or CI so the rectangle is not a matter of opinion.
Apply exactly one indentation step per nesting level and never align continuation lines to look like a block boundary.
Put compound bodies on their own indented line; allow a single simple statement on the header line only when the project's style and its formatter both agree.
When a block has to wrap, fix the cause: extract a named step or add a guard clause instead of nesting one level deeper.
Reformat in a dedicated mechanical commit, never mixed with behaviour changes, and pin the formatter version so the shape does not drift underfoot.
sources: Beck, K., Smalltalk Best Practice Patterns, Prentice Hall (1997) - Chapter 7, Formatting: Rectangular Block (pp. 177-178); Guard Clause (p. 178); Indented Control Flow (p. 175).
